# Hopperlace

> Choose AI for what you want to do — and what matters to you.

Hopperlace helps you choose AI tools and systems that fit your tasks, preferences and values, with evidence you can understand and inspect.

ValueCompass, which you can use today, adds research on the companies behind those tools: their ownership, dependencies and policies. We're also developing independent, hands-on comparisons of the tools themselves.

The aim is to bring these comparisons together with ValueCompass, so you can consider practical fit and values in the same decision.

Focus: independent testing · comparison · informed choice.

## Two parts of one decision

- ValueCompass (available now, https://valuecompass.ai): who is behind it, and does that fit your values? Compare AI options on ownership, control and documented commitments, against the priorities you choose.
- Tool testing (in development): can it do your task, and what will it take? Find out which tools suit a particular task, and what effort, expertise and compromises each one involves.

## ValueCompass — available now (https://valuecompass.ai)

Explore the values behind your AI choices.

Who benefits from the money you spend on AI? What commitments do providers make to the people affected by their technology?

ValueCompass helps you examine the companies behind AI products and compare options against your values. Explore ownership, control, dependencies and documented policies, with sources and clear gaps in the research.

Opens valuecompass.ai. No account needed.

## Tool testing — in development

What makes an AI tool a good fit?

Our comparisons will examine how well an option works for your task, what it asks of you, and the trade-offs involved in choosing it.

### Six questions we ask of every tool

1. Functionality & reliability — does it accomplish your task to the quality you need? How consistently does it work across different cases and repeated attempts, and where does it fail?
2. User effort & expertise — how much setup, guidance, checking and correction does it require? What can you manage yourself, and where is specialist help needed?
3. Oversight & control — can you understand and check what it has done, approve consequential actions, intervene when needed, and recover from mistakes?
4. Maintainability — can you adapt it as your needs change, diagnose problems and make improvements without breaking what already works?
5. Portability & dependencies — what are you committing to? Can you move your data, work or setup elsewhere, and what would switching actually involve?
6. Cost — what does a useful result cost, including subscriptions, usage, retries and the human time involved?

Alongside these practical questions, ValueCompass (available now) helps you examine the ownership, relationships and documented practices behind your choices.

### How we'll test

- Representative tasks, repeated — each tool gets comparable tasks that reflect real use, and each task is run more than once.
- Independent checks — we check the outputs ourselves rather than relying on what the tool reports.
- Successes, failures and repairs — what worked, what broke, and how many attempts it took to fix.
- Money and time, kept apart — monetary cost is recorded separately from the time and human assistance a result required.
- Inspectable evidence — example outputs and the limits of each test are published alongside the advice.

The specific tests depend on the task and the category of tool. The six dimensions are common questions, not an identical checklist or a universal score applied to every product.

### What you'll get

- Options suited to your kind of task.
- The trade-offs that could change the recommendation.
- The evidence behind the advice, so you can check it.

### First planned category: AI app builders

Our first comparisons will apply the framework to tools that build apps from natural-language instructions. The example below shows how each dimension becomes a concrete check.

#### Example test scenario (planned): building and maintaining a booking app

- Decision: which AI app builder suits a small-business owner with limited technical experience?
- Intended outcome: a comparison of which tools suit this user, where specialist help is needed, and the trade-offs involved.
- Proposed checks (not findings; no results yet):
  1. Functionality & reliability — booking and cancellation flows, including conflicting attempts to reserve the same slot.
  2. User effort & expertise — time, correction attempts and technical help needed.
  3. Oversight & control — whether users can see what will change, test before publishing, approve consequential changes and restore an earlier working version.
  4. Maintainability — introducing a new requirement and checking that existing functionality still works.
  5. Portability & dependencies — exporting the project and data, identifying required services, and assessing what moving elsewhere involves.
  6. Cost — tool charges and retries, with development and review time recorded separately.

Note: this describes planned testing, not published results. No comparisons have been published yet.

Hopperlace was founded by Yuyu Shen, a statistically trained data scientist turned product manager with nearly a decade building and evaluating AI systems, including taking AI products from zero to one.

She also built Evidence Synthesis AI (https://www.evidencesynthesisai.com/), which helps research teams use AI to screen studies for systematic reviews. Her research on deference-aware evaluation was accepted at the ICML 2026 Technical AI Governance workshop. She holds CCA-F and CCA-P certifications and writes about technology, agency and better decisions at https://buildwithwhy.com.

## Services (https://hopperlace.ai/services)

Turn business goals into useful AI products.

Hopperlace helps teams clarify what they need to achieve, translate that into a product or system, and evaluate whether it delivers the intended results.

We combine product discovery, system design, hands-on prototyping and meaningful measurement to help you decide what to build, how it should work and what to improve.

You'll work with Yuyu Shen, founder: data science and product analytics at Meta, AI product leadership at Walmart and Beamery, and independent research on AI evaluation. That combination lets her connect business objectives, product decisions, technical design and measurement in a single project. Claude Certified Architect, Professional & Foundations. Paper accepted at the ICML 2026 Technical AI Governance workshop.

### 01 / How we work

One method, whichever project you choose.

1. Define success — agree the intended outcomes, meaningful measures and baseline.
2. Design the system — shape the product, workflow and roles for AI and people.
3. Build and test — prototype the critical parts and test realistic cases.
4. Evaluate and decide — assess results against the agreed measures and recommend next steps.

### 02 / Three kinds of project

Choose where to start. Pick the situation closest to yours to see what the project covers and what you receive. Scope is agreed for each project.

#### A / A goal or problem: define and test an AI opportunity (https://hopperlace.ai/services#define)

Arrive with a business goal or user problem. Work out where AI could help, what to build, and whether it's worthwhile.

"We have a problem to solve or an opportunity to pursue. Where could AI help, what should we build, and how will we know whether it is worthwhile?"

You receive:

- Outcome and product brief: what success means, for whom, and what the product needs to do.
- Workflow and system design: how it should work, what AI does, and where people stay involved.
- Evaluation plan: a baseline, success measures, and how they'll be checked.
- Prototype and findings: a working version tested on realistic cases, where appropriate.

The work, step by step:

1. Clarify the business objective, users' needs and how the work is done today.
2. Define what success means, choose meaningful measures, establish a baseline and agree important constraints.
3. Design the experience, workflow and system, including where AI is appropriate and where people remain involved.
4. Build and test a focused prototype against those criteria, where useful.
5. Recommend what to develop, change or investigate next.

#### B / A provider or tool decision: choose an AI approach (https://hopperlace.ai/services#choose)

Decide which provider, tool or system design to use, based on evidence tested on your cases.

"There are several providers, tools and ways to build this. We need to know which will work for us, what it will cost, and what we'd be committing to."

You receive:

- A comparison of the shortlisted options on your own cases.
- A recommended approach and system design.
- Integration prototypes, where agreed.

The work, step by step:

1. Define the task, constraints and what a useful result looks like.
2. Shortlist providers, tools and system designs, including whether to build, buy or combine.
3. Test the shortlist on your cases, more than once, with integration prototypes where a paper comparison can't answer the question.
4. Compare options across the six evaluation dimensions (see 04 / Evaluation).
5. Recommend an approach, with the trade-offs that could change it.

How we treat evidence: we distinguish published terms and documentation, provider claims, our own test results, and the conclusions we draw from them. Recommendations make clear what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and which trade-offs could change the decision.

- Published terms and documentation — pricing, limits and policies as the provider publishes them.
- Provider claims — what providers say about capability and accuracy.
- Our test results — what we observed running each option on your cases.
- Our conclusions — what we infer from the evidence, marked as judgment.

#### C / An existing feature: improve an existing AI experience (https://hopperlace.ai/services#improve)

Find what is holding it back for real users, then test and make the changes.

"The demo looks promising, and the dashboard looks fine, but real users still struggle, correct the output, or redo the work."

You receive:

- A diagnosis supported by real examples.
- A check on whether your metrics reflect useful outcomes.
- Tested or implemented changes, where agreed.
- Evidence of their effect.

The work, step by step:

1. Review real examples, and agree what success should mean for the people using it.
2. Check whether current metrics reflect useful outcomes, including hidden failures and work passed back to users.
3. Trace the problem across model behavior, the information available, the workflow and the interface.
4. Prototype or implement selected improvements, and compare before and after on the same cases.
5. Hand over test cases your team can rerun, and clear next steps.

### 03 / Experience from previous roles

Work Yuyu led before Hopperlace. Selected examples from Yuyu's previous roles, not Hopperlace client projects.

- Beamery — Defining a new product opportunity. Context: hiring had slowed, while Beamery's offering had focused mainly on recruitment. Yuyu's contribution: recognized that existing AI capabilities could also help companies define roles and skills, opening opportunities in internal mobility and workforce planning; persuaded leadership to explore the direction, secured support for a team and found willing pilot customers. Progress: a new product direction — Dynamic Job Architecture, with willing pilot customers.
- Enjoy Technology — Turning an objective into a working system. Objective: improve delivery productivity by adapting coverage to changing demand and available delivery capacity. Yuyu's contribution: personally built a Python proof-of-concept algorithm for adaptive delivery coverage, then led it into product development as Last Mile Smart Routing. Result: +8–13% visits per vehicle from Last Mile Smart Routing.
- Cleo — Evaluation that guides improvement. Objective: improve the quality of transaction data used by Cleo's AI financial assistant. Yuyu's contribution: led the evaluation strategy for transaction enrichment, working with modeling and data-science teams to prioritize what to measure and improve; as PM for bank connections and transaction data, also owned data-purchasing decisions, the Plaid relationship and evaluation of alternative providers. Result: transaction-enrichment accuracy rose from 56% to 89%.

### 04 / Evaluation

Measure whether it works, and whether it matters. Evaluation covers the whole experience and system, not only the model. It answers two different questions, and a higher task score alone doesn't establish business impact.

1. Does it do the job reliably? Whether the system performs its intended tasks well and consistently, across realistic cases and repeated attempts. Evidence from repeated, representative tests.
2. Does that produce the outcome? Whether those tasks contribute to the outcomes that matter to users and the business. Evidence from real use.

Useful measurement involves: choosing the right metrics — measures that reflect the intended outcome, agreed before testing · spotting misleading proxies — numbers that can improve while users are no better off · counting checking and correction — the human time spent verifying, fixing or redoing the output · interpreting the results — what the evidence supports, and what remains uncertain.

Across the experience and system, we assess: (1) functionality & reliability — whether it does the task on your cases, how consistently across repeated runs, and where it fails · (2) user effort & expertise — the setup, integration, checking and correction your team would take on · (3) oversight & control — whether your team can inspect outputs, approve consequential actions, intervene and recover from errors · (4) maintainability — how readily it adapts as requirements change, without breaking what already works · (5) portability & dependencies — lock-in, data handling, required services, and what switching would involve · (6) cost — usage and licensing, retries, and the staff time spent reviewing and correcting.

### 05 / What a project can look like (illustrative example, not a client project)

A small business wants to turn client briefs and meeting notes into useful project plans.

1. Objective — reduce planning effort while preserving important client requirements.
2. Product / system — drafts a project scope and task plan from the documents; links important details back to their sources; flags missing information; a person reviews and approves the plan.
3. Evaluation — missed requirements; unsupported commitments; whether people can use the plan; total planning effort, including review and correction, compared with the existing process.

Illustrative product behavior: each commitment in the draft points to where it came from. Gaps are flagged rather than filled in, and nothing is shared until a person approves it. Those same behaviors are what the evaluation checks.

### 07 / Working together

Start with one objective, decision, prototype or workflow. Each project is built around a concrete decision, a tested direction or a working artifact your team can use.

1. Agreed before we start — scope, inputs, deliverables, timing and fee are agreed before work begins, around the question the project needs to answer.
2. Hands-on work — discovery, system design, prototyping, evaluation and selected implementation, in whatever mix the question calls for.
3. A clear handoff — prototypes, tests and findings are handed over so your team can carry on. Projects can stand alone or be followed by a small advisory engagement.

Why Hopperlace: the same questions behind our product work. Client projects and Hopperlace's public tool testing, now in development, start from the same questions: what an AI system actually accomplishes, what makes it useful for a particular task and person, and how people can make better choices about it. Client work stays confidential.

### Get in touch

Tell us what you're working on. A few sentences is plenty: an objective or problem you want to clarify, or something you're choosing, building or improving. Add what's uncertain and any timing that matters.
